description: "Caching database queries in PHP with Redis cuts read latency from milliseconds to microseconds. Learn cache aside, TTL tuning, and invalidation."

takeaways:
  - "The cache aside pattern checks Redis first and only runs the real database query on a miss, then stores the result."
  - "Cache data that is read often and written rarely, such as user profiles or product listings, not values that change every request."
  - "Set TTLs by data type, for example 60 seconds for a product price and 86400 seconds for a site setting."
  - "Deleting the cached key on every update removes stale reads immediately instead of waiting for the TTL to expire."
  - "A short lived lock on popular keys lets one request rebuild the value and prevents a cache stampede on the database."

<div id="bx-article">

  <div class="bx-pills">
    <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">PHP</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">Caching</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">Redis</span>
  </div>

  <p class="bx-lede">A database query that takes fifty milliseconds feels instant once. It feels very different once a thousand visitors trigger it every minute. Caching database queries in PHP with Redis is how that same query starts answering in under a millisecond on every repeat.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">01</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="why-caching-database-queries-in-php-with-redis-cuts-read-latency">Why Caching Database Queries in PHP With Redis Cuts Read Latency</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Every database query pays for a network round trip, a query plan, and disk or buffer pool access, even for data that barely changes.</p>

  <p>Redis keeps that same data in memory on a server built for one job: answering key lookups as fast as the network allows. <a href="https://memcached.org/about" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Memcached</a> is the other well known option here, though Redis's richer data structures make it the more common default for new projects today.</p>

  <p>The pattern below, cache aside, is the simplest way to put that speed in front of an existing <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">MySQL</a> or PostgreSQL query without rewriting how the application talks to its database.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">02</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="connecting-to-redis-and-deciding-what-belongs-in-cache">Connecting to Redis and Deciding What Belongs in Cache</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The connection setup is the same <a href="https://pecl.php.net/package/redis" target="_blank" rel="noopener">phpredis</a> extension and pattern covered earlier in this series for rate limiting, just pointed at a different set of keys. <a href="https://packagist.org/packages/predis/predis" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Predis</a> is a pure PHP alternative worth knowing about when the phpredis C extension cannot be installed on a shared host.</p>

  <p>Not every query is worth caching. A value read often and written rarely, like a user profile or a product listing, is a good candidate. A value that changes on every request is not.</p>

  <p><a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/setex/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Redis's own reference for SETEX</a> documents exactly how the expiry argument used throughout this article behaves at the command level.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">redis_connect.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-val">$redis</span> = <span class="tok-kw">new</span> Redis();
<span class="tok-val">$redis</span>->connect(<span class="tok-str">'127.0.0.1'</span>, <span class="tok-val">6379</span>);
<span class="tok-val">$redis</span>->setOption(Redis::OPT_PREFIX, <span class="tok-str">'cache:'</span>);</code></pre>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">03</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="implementing-the-cache-aside-pattern">Implementing the Cache Aside Pattern</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Cache aside checks Redis first. On a miss, it runs the real query, stores the result, and returns it. On a hit, the database is never touched.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">get_user_cached.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">get_user_cached</span>(Redis <span class="tok-val">$redis</span>, PDO <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>, <span class="tok-kw">int</span> <span class="tok-val">$userId</span>): <span class="tok-kw">array</span> {
    <span class="tok-val">$key</span> = <span class="tok-str">"user:$userId"</span>;
    <span class="tok-val">$cached</span> = <span class="tok-val">$redis</span>->get(<span class="tok-val">$key</span>);

    <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">$cached</span> !== <span class="tok-val">false</span>) {
        <span class="tok-kw">return</span> json_decode(<span class="tok-val">$cached</span>, <span class="tok-val">true</span>);
    }

    <span class="tok-val">$stmt</span> = <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->prepare(<span class="tok-str">'SELECT id, name, plan FROM users WHERE id = ?'</span>);
    <span class="tok-val">$stmt</span>->execute([<span class="tok-val">$userId</span>]);
    <span class="tok-val">$user</span> = <span class="tok-val">$stmt</span>->fetch(PDO::FETCH_ASSOC);

    <span class="tok-val">$redis</span>->setex(<span class="tok-val">$key</span>, <span class="tok-val">300</span>, json_encode(<span class="tok-val">$user</span>));
    <span class="tok-kw">return</span> <span class="tok-val">$user</span>;
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>PHP's own <a href="https://www.php.net/manual/en/pdo.prepared-statements.php" target="_blank" rel="noopener">PDO prepared statements documentation</a> covers the parameter binding used above, which stays exactly the same whether or not a cache sits in front of it.</p>

  <p>Running this twice in a row, once cold and once warm, against a query deliberately slowed down to simulate real database latency, shows exactly what that cache hit is worth.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real terminal output of bench.php showing a 49.18 millisecond cold cache read versus a 0.16 millisecond warm cache read, a 307.4x speedup" />
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual timing output from running the cache aside function cold and then warm against the same key.</p>

  <p>That gap only grows under real traffic, since every one of those repeat reads that used to hit the database now costs Redis a fraction of a millisecond instead.</p>

  <div class="bx-table-wrap">
    <table class="bx-table">
      <thead><tr><th>Strategy</th><th>When It Writes to Cache</th><th>Best For</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Cache aside</td><td>On a cache miss, lazily</td><td>Read heavy data with occasional writes</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Read through</td><td>Automatically inside the cache layer</td><td>Apps that want caching hidden from query code</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Write through</td><td>On every write, immediately</td><td>Data that must never serve stale on a read</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">04</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="setting-ttls-based-on-how-stale-data-can-be">Setting TTLs Based on How Stale Data Can Be</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A single global expiry treats a rarely changing setting the same as a price that updates hourly, which is rarely the right tradeoff for either one.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">ttl_by_type.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-val">$ttlSeconds</span> = [
    <span class="tok-str">'user_profile'</span> => <span class="tok-val">3600</span>,
    <span class="tok-str">'product_price'</span> => <span class="tok-val">60</span>,
    <span class="tok-str">'site_setting'</span>  => <span class="tok-val">86400</span>,
];

<span class="tok-val">$redis</span>->setex(<span class="tok-val">$key</span>, <span class="tok-val">$ttlSeconds</span>[<span class="tok-val">$dataType</span>], <span class="tok-val">$payload</span>);</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>A shorter TTL means more database reads but fresher data. A longer TTL means fewer reads but a longer window where a change is not yet visible. <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/caching/best-practices/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">AWS's own caching best practices guide</a> walks through this exact tradeoff in more depth, independent of which cache server is running behind it.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">05</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="invalidating-cache-the-moment-data-changes">Invalidating Cache the Moment Data Changes</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A TTL alone means every update waits out the clock before the cache catches up. Explicit invalidation on write removes that wait entirely.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">update_user_plan.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">update_user_plan</span>(Redis <span class="tok-val">$redis</span>, PDO <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>, <span class="tok-kw">int</span> <span class="tok-val">$userId</span>, <span class="tok-kw">string</span> <span class="tok-val">$newPlan</span>): <span class="tok-kw">void</span> {
    <span class="tok-val">$stmt</span> = <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->prepare(<span class="tok-str">'UPDATE users SET plan = ? WHERE id = ?'</span>);
    <span class="tok-val">$stmt</span>->execute([<span class="tok-val">$newPlan</span>, <span class="tok-val">$userId</span>]);

    <span class="tok-val">$redis</span>->del(<span class="tok-str">"user:$userId"</span>);
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>The next read after that delete finds nothing in Redis, falls back to the database automatically, and quietly repopulates the cache with the fresh value.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real terminal output showing a cache key present after the first read, removed immediately after a plan update, and automatically repopulated after the next read" />
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output confirming a write invalidates the stale key and the following read repopulates it.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">06</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="preventing-cache-stampede-on-popular-keys">Preventing Cache Stampede on Popular Keys</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>When a hot key expires, every request arriving in that same instant can miss the cache together and hit the database all at once.</p>

  <p>A short lived lock lets one request rebuild the value while the rest wait briefly and then read the freshly cached result instead of repeating the same query.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">rebuild_with_lock.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-val">$lockKey</span> = <span class="tok-str">"lock:$key"</span>;

<span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">$redis</span>->set(<span class="tok-val">$lockKey</span>, <span class="tok-val">1</span>, [<span class="tok-str">'nx'</span>, <span class="tok-str">'ex'</span> => <span class="tok-val">5</span>])) {
    <span class="tok-val">$fresh</span> = <span class="tok-fn">run_expensive_query</span>();
    <span class="tok-val">$redis</span>->setex(<span class="tok-val">$key</span>, <span class="tok-val">300</span>, json_encode(<span class="tok-val">$fresh</span>));
    <span class="tok-val">$redis</span>->del(<span class="tok-val">$lockKey</span>);
} <span class="tok-kw">else</span> {
    usleep(<span class="tok-val">50000</span>);
    <span class="tok-kw">return</span> <span class="tok-fn">get_user_cached</span>(<span class="tok-val">$redis</span>, <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>, <span class="tok-val">$userId</span>);
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Only the request that wins the lock ever reaches the database. Every other request briefly waits instead of piling on with a duplicate query. <a href="https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/cdn/what-is-caching/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cloudflare's overview of caching</a> covers this same stampede problem at the edge network layer, where the same lock and wait idea shows up under a different name.</p>

  <ul class="bx-checklist">
    <li><b>Cache reads, invalidate writes:</b> a stale read is usually cheap to fix, a stale write is not.</li>
    <li><b>Vary TTL by data type:</b> a setting that rarely changes can sit far longer than a price.</li>
    <li><b>Delete on update, do not wait for expiry:</b> explicit invalidation removes an entire class of staleness.</li>
    <li><b>Guard hot keys with a short lock:</b> stops a stampede from hitting the database all at once.</li>
    <li><b>Prefix cache keys clearly:</b> keeps cache data separate from anything else sharing the same Redis instance.</li>
  </ul>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">07</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="measuring-whether-caching-is-actually-helping">Measuring Whether Caching Is Actually Helping</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Redis tracks its own hit and miss counts, which is the fastest way to confirm a cache is doing real work rather than sitting mostly empty.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">terminal</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-cm"># check the running hit ratio directly from Redis</span>
redis-cli info stats | grep keyspace</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>A hit ratio that stays low after normal traffic usually means the TTL is too short, the wrong queries were chosen for caching, or invalidation is firing more often than it should.</p>

  <svg width="100%" height="220" viewBox="0 0 800 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a request checking Redis first, serving a cache hit directly, or falling back to the database on a miss and storing the result back in Redis" style="margin:26px 0;">

    <div class="bx-faq">
    <h3 class="bx-h3">Frequently Asked Questions</h3>

    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">1</span><span>What is the simplest way to start caching database queries in PHP with Redis?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Cache aside is the simplest starting point. Check Redis first, run the real query only on a miss, then store the result before returning it.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">2</span><span>How long should a cached value stay valid?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>It depends entirely on how stale the data can safely be. A rarely changing setting can sit for a day, while a price should expire in minutes.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">3</span><span>Is a TTL enough, or does the cache need explicit invalidation too?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>A TTL alone leaves a window where an update is not yet visible. Deleting the key on write removes that window immediately.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">4</span><span>What causes a cache stampede and how is it prevented?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>A popular key expiring lets many requests miss at once. A short lived lock lets one request rebuild it while the rest wait briefly instead of piling on.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">5</span><span>How can a hit ratio that stays low be diagnosed?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Check whether the TTL is too short, whether the wrong queries were chosen for caching, or whether invalidation is firing more often than the data actually changes.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-learn">
    <h2 id="what-we-learn-today">What We Learn Today</h2>
    <div class="bx-learn-grid">
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">1</span><div><h4>Cache aside is the simplest start</h4><p>Check Redis first, query the database only on a miss.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">2</span><div><h4>Not every query deserves caching</h4><p>Read heavy, rarely changing data benefits the most.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">3</span><div><h4>TTL should match data volatility</h4><p>A setting and a price should never share one expiry.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">4</span><div><h4>Invalidate on write, not just on expiry</h4><p>A delete on update removes stale reads immediately.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">5</span><div><h4>Stampedes need a lock</h4><p>One request rebuilds a hot key while others wait briefly.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">6</span><div><h4>Hit ratio tells the real story</h4><p>A low ratio after normal traffic signals a tuning problem.</p></div></div>
    </div>
  </div>

<script>
(function() {
  var items = document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item');

  items.forEach(function(item) {
    var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
    var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');

    item.classList.add('open');
    a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';

    q.addEventListener('click', function() {
      var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
      if (isOpen) {
        item.classList.remove('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = null;
      } else {
        item.classList.add('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
      }
    });
  });
})();
</script>
